description: Common Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2026.

talks.title: Wednesday
talks.teaser: Bundles talks on FHIR OAuth enumeration, Google Cloud service agent escalation, coding agent guardrails and CVE governance.
talks.summary:
This livestream from the BSidesLV Common Ground stage carries several back-to-back sessions. It opens with healthcare interoperability, where a speaker examined the OAuth layer behind FHIR APIs used by EHR and payer systems. The main finding was that error responses in many deployments let an attacker tell valid client IDs from invalid ones. Seven of the fourteen stacks tested showed the issue, and the speaker described a companion scanning tool and vendor disclosures still in progress.

A cloud session followed, showing how Google Cloud service agents can become privilege escalation paths. The researcher presented two case studies: a read-only monitoring user who could reach a privileged Cloud Run endpoint through an uptime check, and an Eventarc configuration that let an attacker obtain a service agent token. The method was to pick a target service, map the primitives it exposes, and find the missing authorization step. A mapping tool for service agent permissions was also introduced. Next, a talk on coding agents covered layered controls such as hooks, sandboxing, deny rules and managed settings, arguing that prompt-injection defense alone will not stop agents from overreaching.

The stream closed with a CVE program panel discussing MITRE's role as a CNA of last resort, the rise of low-quality AI-generated submissions, validation expectations, funding pressure and board governance. For practitioners, the through-line is to test authorization beyond what the console shows, make authentication failures uniform, and scope what automated agents are allowed to do.

talks.title: Tuesday
talks.teaser: Bundles several BSides Las Vegas talks on breach fallout, AI agent identity, MCP server security, and privacy policy.
talks.summary:
This recording covers a run of sessions from one BSides Las Vegas day. It opens with an analysis of small businesses that closed after a cyber incident. The speaker built a list of roughly three dozen companies and examined what actually drove them under, finding that recovery speed, recovery cost, lost customers, and lawsuits mattered more than company size, and that a widely repeated statistic about business closures has no solid basis.

Later sessions focus on AI agents. One presenter proposes giving agents portable cryptographic identities and using fine-grained authorization to decide what each agent may do. The demo is a live multiplayer word game in which agents from separate servers take turns, and unauthorized actions are denied in real time. Another session presents an open-source scanner for Model Context Protocol servers that combines static analysis with dynamic testing, so that a suspected injection path only counts once it is confirmed by running it. A lighter session walks through a company that delegated decisions to AI tools and the problems that followed.

The day also includes an Electronic Frontier Foundation panel covering license plate readers, age verification, interoperability under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, and how to run community security training. A talk on encryption flaws in internet-connected intimate devices and their companion apps closes the block. Practitioners should take away the value of evidence-driven priorities, verifying what agents are permitted to do, and treating surveillance as a harm to be designed against.

talks.title: Monday
talks.teaser: Presents a mixed block of talks on USB dock firmware, encryption policy, post-quantum PKI, drone airspace and dependency risk.
talks.summary:
This Common Ground stream block gathers several short talks rather than a single presentation. The opening segment treats USB docking stations as small embedded computers and shows how a hub controller's firmware update path can be abused through a browser-based updater, since the controller accepts any well-formed 8051 image. A later segment is a policy talk from a long-time digital rights lawyer, who recounts the court fight that freed strong encryption from export controls and argues that privacy acts as a check on power.

Other segments focus on practical engineering. One covers an application security team's attempt to automate CVE fixes and flaky-test repairs in CI, and why interactive LLM sessions with rich context worked better than autonomous bots. A post-quantum PKI lab walkthrough shows how to build a test certificate hierarchy using ML-DSA and ML-KEM on Windows and Linux. A drone airspace talk explains remote ID coverage, sensor limits, and why jamming or kinetic responses are poor choices. A supply chain segment covers malicious package releases, install scripts, and dependency confusion with private registries.

The main takeaways are defensive: pin dependencies, restrict install scripts, monitor critical packages, keep root certificate authorities offline, and treat recurring pipeline failures as a security signal. Depth varies a lot across the block, from policy discussion for general audiences to firmware and cryptography detail.
